storySeeds.title: The Big Dipper’s secret family
storySeeds.summary: Walk the five Dipper stars that were born together (Merak, Phecda, Megrez, Alioth, Mizar & Alcor), with a twist at M40 (a pair that is not a pair, 1.4° from Megrez) and a payoff at the two outsiders, yellow Dubhe and blue-white Alkaid, which drift their own way. Coda: the Coma Star Cluster as a family that has not yet dispersed. All within one 25° patch.

storySeeds.title: Arc to Arcturus, speed on to Spica: how mass sets a star’s fate
storySeeds.summary: Muphrid (a subgiant just starting to swell, a true 3-light-year neighbor of Arcturus) → Arcturus (a Sun-mass giant from the thick disk, the Sun’s future) → optional Groombridge 1830 detour (an even older halo visitor) → Spica (two stars of 11 and 7 solar masses, 12 Myr old, a future supernova). Classic ‘arc to Arcturus’ star-hop from the Dipper handle; the Spring Triangle with Denebola can be the coda.

storySeeds.title: Red, redder, reddest under the Dipper’s handle
storySeeds.summary: Cor Caroli (≈12,000 K, magnetic spotted prototype) → Chara (a near-solar twin, ≈5,900 K) → Arcturus (orange giant, 4,286 K) → La Superba (carbon star, ≈2,700 K, ‘the magnificent’), using Universe Today’s finding directions (a third of the way from Cor Caroli toward Megrez). Teach the Purkinje effect at La Superba and end on where our carbon comes from. Doc 02 §7 story 6 (spring variant).

storySeeds.title: Seeing double, and doubting it, in Boötes
storySeeds.summary: δ Boo (104″ physical pair; its companion is as bright as the Sun would be there) → μ Boo (109″ pair whose faint star is itself a telescopic double) → ν¹/ν² Boo (a 10′ ‘pair’ at 974 and 441 ly: optical) → Izar (looks like a dim Arcturus but is five times farther; luminosity vs brightness) → Arcturus. All within about 15°, Moon-friendly.

historyHook.text: Interferometer images taken between 2016 and 2021 revealed large bright and dark spots on Polaris that change over time.

card.question: How can the North Star help measure the distance to other galaxies?
card.answer: Time a Cepheid’s beat and you know its true power; compare that with how faint it looks and you have its distance, and a nearby, weighable Cepheid like Polaris is where astronomers check that the rule is honest.
card.glance: A steady, pale yellow star almost exactly at the pole, sitting on the edge of a small ring of fainter stars.
card.whyHere: Polaris is more than the pivot of the northern sky; it is also the nearest of a special breed of pulsing star.
card.see: Follow the two end stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl up to Polaris, at the tip of the Little Dipper’s handle. Binoculars show it sitting on a little loop of fainter stars, the Engagement Ring, like the diamond on top. Its pulsing is far too slight for the eye to catch.
card.understand: Polaris is a yellow supergiant, a big, bright aging star, and a Cepheid: it rhythmically swells and shrinks, here every four days, at a rate tied to its true brightness. The rule needs calibrating, and Polaris offers a rare chance. A close partner circles it about every 30 years, and an interferometer, which links telescopes to see fine detail, followed the orbit and weighed Polaris directly at about five Suns.
card.wonder: Close-up images from the CHARA telescope array show bright and dark patches on its surface that come and go.
card.connect: Polaris has not always been the pole star, and Kochab, nearby, once had the job.
card.photoCaption: Survey photos show Polaris as a saturated point among its ring of field stars; its spotted surface appears only in interferometer reconstructions.
card.deeper: Evans et al. (2024) followed the roughly 30-year orbit of the close companion with the CHARA Array and found 5.13 ± 0.28 solar masses; the result depends on the high eccentricity (0.63), and the star is brighter than models predict for that mass. The distance is still argued over: Gaia EDR3 measures the wide companion Polaris B at 7.29 mas (about 448 light-years), Hipparcos gave 7.54 mas for Polaris A, and an HST parallax of Polaris B (Bond et al. 2018) gives 6.26 mas (about 521 light-years). GCVS lists a 3.97-day period and a range of only 1.86–2.13 mag.

card.question: Has Polaris always been the North Star?
card.answer: Polaris is a recent holder of the title, for the slow wobble of Earth’s axis carries the pole among the stars, and in ancient times it lay much nearer Kochab.
card.glance: A bright orange star at the outer end of the Little Dipper’s bowl, beside a fainter white star, Pherkad.
card.whyHere: Kochab is an aging orange giant guarding the pole, and its place in the sky holds a clue to how the sky itself moves.
card.see: Between Polaris and the Big Dipper’s handle shine the two ‘guardians of the pole’. In binoculars Kochab is clearly orange and Pherkad, a few degrees away, white, and a touch of defocus makes the colors easier to judge.
card.understand: Kochab has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a giant about 45 times the Sun’s width, with a cool orange surface near 4,100 K. The pole itself is not fixed: Earth spins like a top, and like a top its axis slowly wobbles, tracing a big circle on the sky over thousands of years. Wherever the axis happens to point, that star becomes the pole star.
card.wonder: Astronomers have found a giant planet, several times Jupiter’s mass, circling this giant star.
card.connect: Polaris, the current pole star, is a very different star holding the same job.
card.photoCaption: Photographs show only an orange point; the planet is known from the star’s regular wobble, not from images.
card.deeper: Hipparcos (2007) gives a parallax of 24.91 ± 0.12 mas, about 131 light-years. A limb-darkened diameter of 10.30 mas (Mozurkewich et al. 2003, via JMDC) at that distance means about 45 solar radii. The NASA Exoplanet Archive lists β UMi b (Lee et al. 2014): a radial-velocity planet with a 522-day period and a minimum mass of about 6 Jupiters. Literature temperatures cluster near 4,000–4,350 K.

historyHook.text: In 2020 astronomers finally detected the faint light of Regulus’s hidden partner: the stripped core of a star that once fed Regulus its gas.

card.question: Why does Regulus spin so fast that it bulges?
card.answer: That partner was once the bigger star, and when it swelled, Regulus pulled away its outer gas and, with it, the spin, leaving the partner a small, hot core.
card.glance: A bright blue-white star at the foot of Leo’s ‘Sickle’, with a faint companion that steady binoculars may show.
card.whyHere: Regulus spins so fast that it is visibly flattened, and the reason lies with a companion nobody could see for decades.
card.see: Regulus is the bright dot at the bottom of the backward question mark of Leo’s head, crisp and blue-white in binoculars. Brace them and look about a tenth of a Moon-width to the north-west for faint Regulus B, a small star that travels with it.
card.understand: Regulus is a hot, young star of about three and a half Suns that turns once in roughly 16 hours, so fast that its equator bulges and runs cooler and dimmer than its poles. Interferometers, which link telescopes to see fine detail, measured the squashed shape directly. A tiny wobble then revealed an unseen partner on a 40-day orbit, and in 2020 astronomers finally caught its faint light: the stripped core of a star.
card.wonder: Spin it much faster and Regulus would begin flinging gas off its equator; it already turns at about 86% of that limit.
card.connect: Nearby, a cool orange giant makes a vivid color contrast.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a single bright point; the flattened shape was measured with linked telescopes (CHARA), not imaged directly.
card.deeper: McAlister et al. (2005) combined CHARA interferometry with spectroscopy: projected rotation 317 ± 3 km/s, an equatorial speed about 86% of break-up, and radii of about 4.2 (equator) and 3.1 (pole) solar radii. Gies et al. (2008) found a 40-day orbit from tiny radial-velocity shifts, and Gies et al. (2020) detected the companion’s own spectrum: a pre-white dwarf of about 0.31 solar masses, as predicted for a star stripped by mass transfer. WDS lists Regulus B (K2 V) 176″ away; it has its own faint partner. Hipparcos parallax 41.13 ± 0.35 mas (79 light-years).

card.question: What will the Sun look like in old age?
card.answer: In billions of years the Sun will look much like Arcturus does tonight, an orange-gold giant with a cooler surface but far more light.
card.glance: The brightest star of spring, a strong orange-gold light in Boötes at the end of the curve you follow from the Big Dipper’s handle.
card.whyHere: Arcturus is an old orange giant racing through our neighborhood, and it offers a preview of the Sun’s own old age.
card.see: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper’s handle away from the bowl to the first bright star, Arcturus, the brightest in Boötes. Its orange-gold is obvious in binoculars. Carry the same curve on to blue-white Spica and compare.
card.understand: Arcturus weighs about the same as the Sun but is billions of years older, and it has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 25 times the Sun’s width. Its surface has cooled to about 4,300 K, yet all that glowing surface makes it shine about 200 times as brightly as the Sun. It is also poor in heavy elements and crosses our sky fast, at about 122 kilometers per second, the mark of a visitor from the galaxy’s older, thicker disk.
card.wonder: In 1933 its starlight switched on the lights of the Chicago World’s Fair.
card.connect: A star ten times heavier, Spica, will end far more violently.
card.photoCaption: Survey photos saturate on Arcturus and lose its color; the binocular view shows the orange tint better than these plates.
card.deeper: Ramírez & Allende Prieto (2011) found Teff 4286 ± 30 K, log g 1.66, [Fe/H] −0.52, mass 1.08 ± 0.06 solar masses, radius 25.4 solar radii and an age of about 7.1 billion years. Its Hipparcos parallax is 88.83 ± 0.54 mas (36.7 light-years). The proper motion, about 2.3″ per year, shifts it by a full Moon-width in roughly 800 years. Arcturus and other stars sharing its motion (the ‘Arcturus group’) were proposed as debris of a disrupted satellite galaxy (Navarro et al. 2004); that origin remains debated.

card.question: What decides whether a star ends quietly or in an explosion?
card.answer: Mass decides, and Spica’s bigger star, about 11 Suns, is heavy enough to end as a supernova, while Sun-weight Arcturus will fade quietly into a white dwarf.
card.glance: A brilliant blue-white star alone in the low southern sky at the bottom of Virgo.
card.whyHere: Spica is two heavy, very hot stars in a four-day orbit, so close they pull each other out of round, and their weight seals their fate.
card.see: From Arcturus, continue the Dipper-handle curve about as far again to a lone, brilliant blue-white star. It stays one sharp point, since no telescope can split the pair. Compare its icy color with Arcturus’s orange.
card.understand: Spica is a pair of hot stars of about 11 and 7 Suns, weighed by tracking their orbit in 1,731 spectra. Heavy stars burn their fuel disproportionately fast, so this pair is only about 12 million years old, while Arcturus is billions of years old. The two orbit so tightly that tides stretch each into an egg shape, and the light wobbles as the eggs turn.
card.wonder: Arcturus looks brighter to your eye, yet Spica’s bigger star is the one that will explode.
card.connect: Back in the Big Dipper, a family of stars has stayed together for about 400 million years.
card.photoCaption: No photograph separates the two stars; their shapes are known from spectra and from tiny, regular changes in brightness.
card.deeper: Tkachenko et al. (2016) combined 1,731 high-resolution spectra with space photometry: masses 11.43 ± 1.15 and 7.21 ± 0.75 solar masses, radii 7.47 and 3.74 solar radii, a primary temperature of 25,300 ± 500 K, an orbital period of 4.0145 days and an age of 12.5 ± 1 million years. One of the primary’s β Cephei pulsation modes is an exact multiple of the orbital frequency, a tidally excited oscillation. GCVS lists the light variation (ellipsoidal plus β Cep) at about 0.1 mag. Hipparcos parallax: 13.06 ± 0.70 mas (about 250 light-years).

card.question: Are Mizar and Alcor a real pair, or just lined up?
card.answer: Most likely a real family of six stars, born with most of the Big Dipper about 400 million years ago; their motions agree closely enough to make the bond likely, though not yet proven.
card.glance: Bright Mizar and fainter Alcor at the bend of the Big Dipper’s handle, a pair you can split by eye.
card.whyHere: Mizar and Alcor are the classic first double star, a pair you can split with your eyes alone.
card.see: Look at the middle star of the Big Dipper’s handle, and keen eyes will catch little Alcor beside it. Binoculars spread them less than half a Moon-width apart, with a fainter star making a small triangle. Mizar’s own close companion needs a telescope.
card.understand: Mizar and Alcor lie roughly 80 to 90 light-years away and drift through space together. Each is itself multiple, and Mizar’s story is a classic: in 1889 Edward Pickering noticed that its spectral lines periodically doubled as two unseen stars swung toward and away from us in turn, the first binary found by its spectrum alone. Alcor’s small red companion turned up only in 2009, and the whole group shares its motion with most of the Big Dipper.
card.wonder: For centuries people tested their eyesight on this pair, long before anyone knew it held six stars.
card.connect: Mizar’s siblings are spread across the Dipper, and two Dipper stars are not family at all.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows Mizar, Alcor and the fainter third star much as binoculars do, but with harder points and no color.
card.deeper: Mamajek et al. (2010) imaged Alcor B, a ~0.3 solar-mass star 1.1″ from Alcor, and estimated the Mizar–Alcor separation at 0.36 ± 0.19 pc; their space motions agree only marginally (6% probability), so the sextuple is likely rather than proven. WDS lists Mizar AB at 14.4″ and A–Alcor at 715″. Pickering’s 1890 report of Mizar A’s periodically doubling lines founded spectroscopic binaries. Jones et al. (2015) dated the Ursa Major moving group at 414 ± 23 million years from CHARA interferometry of its A stars, including Alcor (1.84 solar masses). Hipparcos parallax of Mizar A: 38.0 ± 1.7 mas.

card.question: How can a star’s surface be blotched with different elements?
card.answer: In a star calm enough to let its elements sort themselves, even a weak magnetic field can gather them into patches that rotate in and out of view, flickering its light ever so slightly.
card.glance: The brightest Big Dipper star, first in the handle next to the bowl, plain white and steady in binoculars.
card.whyHere: Alioth looks like an ordinary white star, but its surface is blotched with unusual elements, and it is a sibling in the Dipper’s family.
card.see: Alioth is the handle star touching the Big Dipper’s bowl, white and steady in binoculars; its light changes by only about two percent as it turns. Glide along the handle to Mizar and Alcor to take in three family members in one sweep.
card.understand: Alioth is a hot white star born with the Ursa Major family. Its outer layers are unusually calm, so some elements sink under gravity while others are pushed upward by the light streaming out, and a weak magnetic field herds them into patches. Astronomers mapped those patches by watching how each element’s lines in the spectrum shift and change shape as the star turns every five days.
card.wonder: It belongs to the class of spotted stars named after Cor Caroli, just below the handle.
card.connect: Alioth is family, but Dubhe and Alkaid, at the Dipper’s two ends, are not.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a single white point; the spots are mapped from changes in its spectrum as it rotates.
card.deeper: GCVS classes ε UMa as an α² CVn (ACV) variable with a period of 5.0887 days and a range of only 1.76–1.78 mag. Shulyak et al. (2010) reproduced most of its light variation from Doppler-imaging maps of several elements; its dipole field is weak, a few hundred gauss at most, among the weakest of the magnetic chemically peculiar stars. King et al. (2003) count it in the nucleus of the Ursa Major group, dated to 414 ± 23 million years by Jones et al. (2015). Hipparcos parallax: 39.51 ± 0.20 mas (about 83 light-years).

card.question: Is the Big Dipper one family of stars?
card.answer: Most of it is, but not Dubhe: the two pointers look like partners, but they are strangers, for Merak belongs to the Dipper’s family while Dubhe is a passer-by half again as far away.
card.glance: The bright yellow-orange pointer star at the top of the Big Dipper’s bowl.
card.whyHere: Dubhe points the way to Polaris alongside Merak, and the two look like a matched team.
card.see: Dubhe is the upper pointer star of the Big Dipper’s bowl, and Merak, the lower one, is five degrees away. In binoculars Dubhe is yellow-orange and Merak white, so sweep between them a few times. Dubhe’s true companion is far too close to see.
card.understand: Dubhe is a giant that has finished burning hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 26 times the Sun’s width, cooling to a yellow-orange glow. Astronomers sort family from strangers with two measurements: distance, from parallax, and motion, from both the drift across the sky and the speed along our line of sight. Five of the Dipper’s stars pass both tests together, and Dubhe fails.
card.wonder: The Dipper is slowly changing shape, because its two end stars drift differently from the family in the middle.
card.connect: At the far end of the handle, Alkaid is the other outsider, with the opposite color.
card.photoCaption: Photos show only a bright point; the close companion was found by careful measurement, not imaging.
card.deeper: King et al. (2003) re-examined membership of the Ursa Major group using Hipparcos parallaxes and new radial velocities; Merak, Phecda, Megrez, Alioth, Mizar and Alcor are members, while Dubhe and Alkaid are not (summarized by Croswell). Hipparcos gives 26.54 ± 0.48 mas (about 123 light-years). A limb-darkened diameter of 6.42 ± 0.04 mas (Baines et al. 2018, via JMDC) implies about 26 solar radii. Dubhe is a G9 III giant with an A-type companion 0.8″ away (WDS BU 1077 AB).

teffK.note: BCD bolometric-flux method, 17,870 ± 1,060 K

radiusRsun.note: θ 0.832 mas × Hipparcos distance 31.9 pc

superlatives.claim: the hottest of the seven Big Dipper stars

card.question: Why is the star at the end of the Dipper’s handle blue-white?
card.answer: At three times the Sun’s surface temperature Alkaid glows blue-white, a young, heavy star that shares the Dipper’s outline but not its family.
card.glance: The bright blue-white star at the very end of the Big Dipper’s handle.
card.whyHere: Alkaid is the hottest Dipper star and, like Dubhe, an outsider to the family.
card.see: Alkaid ends the Big Dipper’s handle, crisply blue-white against yellow-orange Dubhe at the far end. About three and a half degrees south-west, under dark skies, the Whirlpool Galaxy is a faint smudge for patient eyes.
card.understand: Alkaid’s surface is about 17,900 K, three times hotter than the Sun’s. That temperature was read from a telltale step in its spectrum, a sharp drop in the ultraviolet whose size and position depend on how hot the gas is. Hot stars are heavy and burn their fuel quickly, so Alkaid is young as stars go, and it travels a different way from the five family stars in the middle.
card.wonder: The Dipper’s two ends are a hot youngster and a cool elder, with a true family between them.
card.connect: From hot and blue here to the cool, red end of the scale: La Superba.
card.photoCaption: Photographs record Alkaid as a white point; its blue tint is easier to sense when you compare it with Dubhe in binoculars.
card.deeper: Zorec et al. (2009) give an effective temperature of 17,870 ± 1,060 K and an angular diameter of 0.83 mas from the Balmer-discontinuity (BCD) method; at the Hipparcos distance (31.38 ± 0.24 mas, about 104 light-years) that is roughly 2.9 solar radii. Rapid rotation makes single-number temperatures approximate. King et al. (2003) list Alkaid as a non-member of the Ursa Major group.

card.question: Why is La Superba one of the reddest stars in the sky?
card.answer: It is a carbon star: soot-like molecules at its surface block blue light and let only deep red escape, which is why Angelo Secchi, a pioneer of sorting stars by their spectra, named it ‘the superb one’.
card.glance: A modest star that turns out to be one of the deepest orange-red points in the sky, between Cor Caroli and the Big Dipper’s bowl.
card.whyHere: La Superba is a dying giant in Canes Venatici, faint to the eye but glowing like an ember in binoculars.
card.see: From Cor Caroli, below the Big Dipper’s handle, head about a third of the way toward Megrez. Faint to the eye, La Superba is obvious in binoculars as a glowing red-orange ember, and red stars seem to brighten the longer you stare.
card.understand: Late in life a giant like this burns helium in thin shells around its spent core, and churning currents carry freshly made carbon up to the surface. In its cool atmosphere, about 2,700 K, carbon-rich molecules and soot absorb blue light. The star is also shedding gas and dust, and infrared satellites found a vast shell of it piling up where the star’s wind runs into the surrounding gas.
card.wonder: The carbon in your body was forged in stars like this long before the Sun was born.
card.connect: Cor Caroli, a few degrees away, is hot and white: the other end of the stellar thermometer.
card.photoCaption: Survey plates wash out its color; binoculars show the red better than this photo.
card.deeper: Lambert et al. (1986) derived an effective temperature of about 2,720 K. GCVS classes Y CVn as a semiregular (SRb) variable with V 4.86–7.32; Universe Today describes a cycle of roughly 160 days on top of a longer one of several years. The DEATHSTAR distance catalog (Andriantsaralaza et al. 2022) gives 249 +25/−22 pc (about 810 light-years), while the Gaia EDR3 parallax suggests nearer 1,000. IRAS and ISO found a detached dust shell about 0.9 pc across; Libert et al. (2007) model it as wind material piling up where it meets the surrounding gas.

card.question: How can a magnetic field paint spots on a star?
card.answer: Its strong field pins certain elements in place, and the star’s slow spin, one turn every five and a half days, carries those patches in and out of view, nudging its brightness up and down.
card.glance: A white star alone under the Big Dipper’s handle, with a faint partner that braced 10× binoculars may show almost touching it.
card.whyHere: Cor Caroli is the star that named a whole class of magnetic, spotted stars, and it is also a testing binocular double.
card.see: Cor Caroli is the brightest star below the Big Dipper’s handle, in Canes Venatici. Hold 10× binoculars very steady and look for a much fainter companion right beside it; in 7× it usually stays merged.
card.understand: The brighter star is hot and white, with a strong, lopsided magnetic field that holds elements such as silicon and europium in large patches. Astronomers mapped that field by measuring how its light is polarized, the direction in which the light waves vibrate, which magnetic fields alter in a telltale way. The map looks like a tilted bar magnet dotted with smaller, stronger spots.
card.wonder: Alioth, in the Dipper’s handle above, belongs to the same class and so carries Cor Caroli’s name.
card.connect: North to La Superba, the stellar thermometer runs from white-hot to deep red.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo separates the two stars clearly; in hand-held binoculars the pair is much harder.
card.deeper: GCVS lists α² CVn as the ACV prototype: period 5.47 days, range 2.84–2.98 mag. Kochukhov & Wade (2010) mapped its field in all four Stokes parameters and found a global dipole-like field plus localized high-field spots, along with iron and chromium abundance maps. WDS lists the pair STF 1692 AB at 19.2″ (magnitudes 2.85 and 5.52). Gaia EDR3 gives 30.61 mas for α¹ (about 107 light-years) and 32.72 mas for α² (about 100 light-years); Hipparcos gave 28.41 mas for α².

card.question: How can a star fade to a five-hundredth of its brightness and recover?
card.answer: The star dims far less than it seems; its cooling atmosphere shifts the light out of the colors our eyes can see, cutting the visible glow more than 500-fold before the next swell brings it back.
card.glance: A red giant near Regulus that brightens and fades enormously over about ten months, so it may be easy, faint or invisible tonight.
card.whyHere: R Leonis is a dying giant whose brightness swings by hundreds of times, and you can follow it through the year.
card.see: R Leo lies about five degrees west of Regulus, the star at the foot of Leo’s Sickle, and an AAVSO finder chart shows the field. Near its peak it is an easy orange-red binocular star; near its low point it drops out of reach.
card.understand: R Leonis is a Mira star, a giant in its last stage of life that swells and shrinks, here every 310 days. Its total output changes far less than its visible light: as the outer layers cool, molecules form and block the visible light while much of the energy slips out as infrared. Each pulse also lifts gas and dust off the surface into space.
card.wonder: Its light takes over three centuries to reach you, so you see it as it was around 1700.
card.connect: Regulus, nearby, is a hot, young, fast-spinning star beside this cool, dying one.
card.photoCaption: Any photo shows R Leo at one moment of its cycle; tonight it may look very different.
card.deeper: GCVS lists R Leo as a Mira variable with a range of V 4.4–11.3 and a period of 309.95 days; a 6.9-magnitude swing is a factor of about 575 in visible light, although its total light output changes far less because much of it moves into the infrared. The DEATHSTAR distance catalog (Andriantsaralaza et al. 2022) gives 100 ± 5 pc (about 330 light-years), from the Mira period–luminosity relation; the Hipparcos parallax is too uncertain to help.

eventDependent.note: Its brightness depends on where it is in its 310-day cycle; check AAVSO for its current magnitude before looking.

historyHook.text: Observers in the early 1700s timed its cycle at about 495 days; two centuries later it had shortened to about 385 days.

card.question: Can a star change its own heartbeat?
card.answer: It can, and R Hydrae has: perhaps a brief flare of helium burning deep inside made the star shrink and quicken, a heartbeat altered by an upheaval in its core.
card.glance: A red pulsating giant beside γ Hydrae, at its best a naked-eye star and at its faintest beyond binoculars.
card.whyHere: R Hydrae is a dying giant whose pulse has been timed by observers for three centuries.
card.see: Start at γ Hydrae, the brightest star in this part of Hydra, well below Spica. R Hya lies about two and a half degrees east, often in the same field; near maximum it is obviously orange-red, but for part of its cycle it fades out of reach, so check AAVSO first.
card.understand: R Hydrae is a giant in its last stage of life, pulsing slowly and shedding gas. The clue to its change came from patience rather than technology: astronomers gathered three centuries of observations, from the early 1700s on, and found the cycle shrinking from about 495 days to about 385 by the mid-1900s. Its spectrum also shows technetium, an element with no stable form, which must have been made inside the star recently.
card.wonder: Its present period, about 389 days, has stayed nearly constant since the mid-twentieth century.
card.connect: Steady γ Hydrae beside it shows the calmer giant stage that comes before this one.
card.photoCaption: A photograph catches R Hya at one moment of its cycle; tonight it may be far brighter or fainter.
card.deeper: Zijlstra, Bedding & Mattei (2002) assembled about three centuries of observations: the period was about 495 days before 1770 and declined to roughly 380–385 days by about 1950, staying near that since. They discuss both a helium-shell flash (thermal pulse) and envelope relaxation; the flash interpretation is common but not settled. GCVS lists V 3.5–10.9, P = 388.87 days and spectral type M6e–M9eS(Tc), the Tc marking technetium. DEATHSTAR (Andriantsaralaza et al. 2022): 126 +3/−2 pc, about 410 light-years.

eventDependent.note: Its brightness depends on where it is in its 389-day cycle; check AAVSO for its current magnitude before looking.

card.question: What turns a dying giant deep red?
card.answer: Its own carbon, dredged up from deep inside, filters X Cancri’s light until mostly red is left.
card.glance: A vivid red-orange star a few degrees south-east of the Beehive Cluster, easy in binoculars once you know the field.
card.whyHere: X Cancri is a dying giant just off the Beehive, one of the redder stars within binocular reach.
card.see: From the Beehive, the misty patch in Cancer between Regulus and the Gemini twins, move about four and a half degrees south-east. X Cnc stands out by color, a warm red-orange that deepens the longer you look, and its brightness changes over months.
card.understand: Like La Superba, X Cancri is an old giant whose core is spent and now burns helium in thin shells. Churning currents bring freshly made carbon to the surface, and at about 2,600 K carbon molecules in its atmosphere soak up blue and green light. Its color index, a measure of how much brighter it is in yellow light than in blue, is among the largest of any binocular star.
card.wonder: It looks like the Beehive’s neighbor but lies far behind the cluster.
card.connect: La Superba in Canes Venatici is its brighter carbon-star cousin.
card.photoCaption: This ALMA image shows a different carbon star in radio light; X Cancri itself appears only as a red point.
card.deeper: Lambert et al. (1986) derived an effective temperature of about 2,625 K. GCVS lists X Cnc as a semiregular SRb variable, V 5.52–7.50, with a period of about 193 days and spectral type C5,4. The DEATHSTAR catalog (Andriantsaralaza et al. 2022) gives 332 +41/−36 pc, about 1,080 light-years. Its B−V color index of about 3.2 makes it one of the redder stars within binocular reach.

card.question: What is the most common kind of star near the Sun?
card.answer: Red dwarfs like this one: small, cool and dim, so dim that one of the nearest stars to the Sun needs binoculars to be seen at all.
card.glance: A dim, faintly orange point you would never notice, yet one of the Sun’s closest neighbors.
card.whyHere: Lalande 21185 is one of the Sun’s nearest neighbors, yet you need binoculars to see it.
card.see: Use a detailed chart: it lies below the Big Dipper’s bowl, about four and a half degrees south of 47 Ursae Majoris. In binoculars it is a dim, faintly orange point, no different at first glance from hundreds of distant stars.
card.understand: Red dwarfs are small, cool stars with a fraction of the Sun’s mass, burning fuel so slowly that they will outlast every other kind of star. This one is only about four-tenths of the Sun’s width, measured with an interferometer, and Gaia’s parallax puts it 8.3 light-years away. Most of the Sun’s nearest neighbors are like this, so the naked-eye sky, full of rare powerful stars seen from afar, gives a misleading picture of what stars are usually like.
card.wonder: Two planets have been found orbiting it, and the inner one circles in under two weeks.
card.connect: Groombridge 1830, another nearby Ursa Major star, is a visitor from the galaxy’s ancient halo.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an ordinary faint star; its planets were found only from the star’s tiny wobble.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 gives a parallax of 392.75 ± 0.03 mas (8.30 light-years). Interferometry (Boyajian et al. 2012) measured 1.43 mas, about 0.39 solar radii. It moves 4.8″ per year across the sky and approaches at about 85 km/s (SIMBAD). The NASA Exoplanet Archive lists two radial-velocity planets: b (Díaz et al. 2019; 12.9 days, minimum mass about 2.7 Earths) and c (Rosenthal et al. 2021; about 2,950 days). Literature temperatures span about 3,430–3,830 K.

card.question: Why is Groombridge 1830 racing through our neighborhood?
card.answer: It is not in our lane at all, but on a steep, looping orbit through the galaxy’s ancient halo that happens to carry it through the Sun’s neighborhood right now.
card.glance: A faint yellowish star in a quiet corner of Ursa Major, findable in binoculars with a chart.
card.whyHere: Groombridge 1830 looks like an ordinary faint star, yet it is crossing our neighborhood at about 300 kilometers per second.
card.see: Use a chart: it lies about 16 degrees due south of Phecda, the Big Dipper’s bowl star nearest the handle. In binoculars it is a faint yellowish point with no hint of its speed.
card.understand: Most stars near the Sun circle the galaxy with us in its flat disk, like cars in the same lanes. Groombridge 1830 loops through the halo, the old, thin swarm of stars around the disk, so it cuts across our lane at high speed: Gaia sees it creep about 7 arcseconds a year across the sky, enormous for a star 30 light-years away. Its iron, about a twentieth of the Sun’s, shows it formed early, before generations of stars had enriched the galaxy’s gas.
card.wonder: It crosses the width of the full Moon on the sky in about 250 years.
card.connect: Arcturus is another older visitor passing through, from the galaxy’s thicker disk.
card.photoCaption: Photographs show an ordinary faint star; its motion is revealed only by comparing images taken years apart.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3: parallax 109.03 ± 0.02 mas (29.9 light-years) and proper motion 7.06″ per year; with SIMBAD’s radial velocity of −98 km/s the heliocentric space velocity is about 320 km/s. Literature metallicities cluster at [Fe/H] ≈ −1.3 to −1.4 (SIMBAD compilation), about one-twentieth of the Sun’s iron. Interferometry (Karovicova et al. 2020, via JMDC) gives 0.597 mas, about 0.59 solar radii: a metal-poor dwarf somewhat smaller than the Sun.

historyHook.text: In 2024 the Webb telescope found signs of a thick atmosphere on 55 Cancri e, probably supplied by its magma ocean.

card.question: What is it like on a planet that circles its star in under a day?
card.answer: 55 Cancri e orbits so close that its surface is probably a sea of lava, and in 2024 the Webb telescope found hints of a thick atmosphere rising from it.
card.glance: A faint yellowish star in northern Cancer, easy in binoculars once you know where to look.
card.whyHere: 55 Cancri has five known planets, including a scorching rocky world whose year is shorter than a day.
card.see: 55 Cnc lies about nine degrees north-north-east of the Beehive Cluster in Cancer. In binoculars it is a pale yellowish point, just visible to the naked eye from a very dark site.
card.understand: 55 Cancri is a little cooler and smaller than the Sun, about 41 light-years away. Its planets were found from the tiny wobble they cause in the star’s motion, and the innermost, 55 Cancri e, also passes in front of the star, dimming it slightly, which reveals its size: about twice Earth’s width. Mass from the wobble and size from the shadow together give its density, which is that of rock.
card.wonder: A year on 55 Cancri e lasts under 18 hours.
card.connect: τ Boötis, near Arcturus, is another nearby star with a giant planet in a tight orbit.
card.photoCaption: No photograph shows these planets; every one was found from the star’s motion, and e also by its passages in front of the star.
card.deeper: The NASA Exoplanet Archive lists five planets: b (14.65 days; Butler et al. 1997), c (44.4 days), d (about 4,800 days, minimum mass about 3.9 Jupiters), e (0.737 days, about 8 Earth masses and 1.9 Earth radii) and f (260.6 days; Fischer et al. 2008). A JWST emission spectrum (Hu et al. 2024, reported by Eos) favors a secondary atmosphere rich in carbon dioxide or monoxide over bare rock. Gaia EDR3 parallax 79.45 mas (41.1 light-years); the red dwarf 55 Cnc B lies 85″ away (WDS).

card.question: Can a giant planet orbit closer to its star than Mercury does?
card.answer: τ Boötis’s planet does, weighing about six Jupiters yet racing around its star faster than any planet of ours, one of the first discoveries to show that other planetary systems can be very unlike ours.
card.glance: A pale yellow-white star about seven degrees west of Arcturus, easy in binoculars.
card.whyHere: τ Boötis hosts one of the first planets found around a Sun-like star, a giant racing around it in three days.
card.see: From Arcturus in Boötes, sweep about seven degrees west to a modest yellow-white star, clearly whiter than orange Arcturus. Its red-dwarf companion is far too close and faint for binoculars.
card.understand: τ Boötis is a little heavier and hotter than the Sun. Its planet was found in 1996 from the regular shift of the star’s spectral lines, back and forth every 3.3 days as the planet swings the star around. That rhythm, together with the star’s mass, puts the planet far closer than Mercury is to the Sun, and the pull between the two may be strong enough to make the star’s outer layers turn in step with it.
card.wonder: Its magnetic field flips north and south again and again, far faster than the Sun’s.
card.connect: Not far away, 70 Virginis hosts a giant planet announced the same year.
card.photoCaption: The planet has never been photographed; its presence is read from the star’s regular wobble.
card.deeper: The NASA Exoplanet Archive lists τ Boo b with a period of 3.312 days and a minimum mass of about 5.95 Jupiters, discovered by radial velocities (Butler et al. 1997, announced 1996). Spectropolarimetry (Fares et al. 2009) caught a second reversal of the star’s large-scale magnetic polarity within a short span. Gaia EDR3 parallax: 64.05 mas (50.9 light-years). WDS lists τ Boo B, an M2 dwarf, 1.5″ away.

card.question: What would our Sun look like seen from another star?
card.answer: It would look like Chara, a plain, pale yellow point barely visible to the naked eye, with nothing to suggest it might warm a world of its own.
card.glance: A faint yellowish star in Canes Venatici near La Superba, easy in binoculars and barely visible to the eye under dark skies.
card.whyHere: Chara is a near-twin of the Sun 27 light-years away, our own star seen from outside.
card.see: Chara lies about four and a half degrees south-south-west of La Superba, below the Big Dipper’s handle. Put each in the field in turn, pale yellow Chara and then deep red La Superba; Chara looks unremarkable, just as the Sun would from here.
card.understand: Chara has almost the Sun’s surface temperature and size, and slightly less iron. Its width was measured directly by an interferometer and comes out at about one solar diameter. Like the Sun it shines by fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, a steady stage lasting billions of years, which makes it a natural target in searches for Earth-like planets.
card.wonder: The light reaching you left Chara just after the first planets around Sun-like stars were found.
card.connect: La Superba, close by, is a star far along a later, very different stage of life.
card.photoCaption: Photographs show a plain yellow-white point, which is exactly the lesson: a Sun-like star is unremarkable from afar.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 118.49 ± 0.20 mas (27.5 light-years). Literature effective temperatures span about 5,650–6,010 K and recent metallicities are [Fe/H] ≈ −0.2 (SIMBAD compilation). Interferometry (Baines et al. 2018, via JMDC) gives 1.13 mas, about 1.0 solar radii. At this distance the Sun (absolute magnitude about 4.8) would appear near magnitude 4.5, close to Chara’s own 4.3.

card.question: Why is a pair of plain stars in Messier’s catalog of nebulae?
card.answer: It got there by honest mistake: Messier was looking for a nebula, recorded what he actually saw, and the two stars he found are not even a real pair.
card.glance: Two faint stars side by side just north-east of Megrez, Messier’s 40th ‘nebula’ that never was.
card.whyHere: Messier 40 is a famous mistake: two stars that look like a pair but lie at very different distances.
card.see: From Megrez, where the Big Dipper’s handle meets the bowl, move about one and a half degrees north-east. In 10×50s two faint points sit close together, nearly equal in brightness; brace the binoculars, because they are near the suburban limit.
card.understand: In 1764 Messier went hunting for a fuzzy object reported by Hevelius above the back of the Great Bear, found only this pair, and listed them anyway as number 40. A century later the pair was listed again as a double star, Winnecke 4. Gaia’s parallaxes finally showed that one lies about 470 light-years away and the other more than twice as far, like a near streetlight and a far one seeming to stand side by side.
card.wonder: A pair of strangers has held a place in the most famous catalog of nebulae for over 250 years.
card.connect: Mizar and Alcor, nearby, look no more connected, yet they are a real family.
card.photoCaption: This survey image is magnified about five times more than a binocular view; in binoculars the two stars nearly touch.
card.deeper: Messier logged the pair in 1764 while looking for Hevelius’s ‘nebula’ above the back of the Great Bear; Friedrich Winnecke cataloged it as a double in 1863, and John Mallas linked it to Messier’s note in 1966 (Sky & Telescope, Bob King 2025). WDS gives a separation of 53.2″ and magnitudes 9.7 and 10.2. Gaia EDR3 parallaxes are 3.22 mas for HD 238107 (about 1,010 light-years) and 6.93 mas for HD 238108 (about 470 light-years), so the ‘double’ is purely optical.

card.question: How big is the lonely orange star at Hydra’s heart?
card.answer: Big enough that, in the Sun’s place, Alphard’s surface would reach about two-thirds of the way to Mercury’s orbit.
card.glance: A lone orange star in an empty stretch of sky south-west of Regulus, the heart of Hydra.
card.whyHere: Alphard is a lone orange giant in a dark patch of sky, an uncluttered lesson in color and size.
card.see: Look about 20 degrees south-west of Regulus for the only bright star in a wide, empty region; its Arabic name means ‘the solitary one’. In binoculars it is a rich orange, so swing to blue-white Regulus and back.
card.understand: Alphard has used up the hydrogen in its core, swollen, and cooled to about 4,200 K, so its light leans red. Its size was measured with an interferometer: the disk spans less than a hundredth of an arcsecond, and at its distance of about 180 light-years that works out to more than 50 times the Sun’s width. Glowing from all that surface, it gives out several hundred times the Sun’s light.
card.wonder: Alphard’s light left it about 180 years ago, around the time of the first photographs.
card.connect: Regulus, up in Leo, is a hot young star to set beside this cool giant.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows how empty Alphard’s surroundings are; the star itself is a saturated blob.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 18.09 ± 0.18 mas (about 180 light-years). A limb-darkened diameter of 9.36 mas (Cruzalèbes et al. 2013, via JMDC) at that distance gives about 56 solar radii, roughly 0.26 au, compared with Mercury’s 0.39 au. Literature temperatures span about 4,030–4,400 K (SIMBAD compilation); with 4,190 K the luminosity is near 860 Suns.

card.question: Is the faint star beside Algieba its companion?
card.answer: 40 Leonis only lines up by chance, and Algieba’s real partner is a second golden giant, far too close for binoculars.
card.glance: A golden star in Leo’s mane, with a fainter whitish star a third of a degree to the south.
card.whyHere: Algieba is a golden double for telescopes, and in binoculars it seems to come with a ready-made companion.
card.see: Algieba is the brightest star of Leo’s Sickle after Regulus. Binoculars cannot split its two golden giants, so notice instead 40 Leonis, a fainter whitish star about a third of a degree south that looks like a companion.
card.understand: Algieba is really two orange-gold giants orbiting each other far apart, with surfaces around 4,500 K, cooler than the Sun’s. The brighter one also has a giant planet at least about nine times Jupiter’s mass, found from the star’s gentle wobble. 40 Leonis, meanwhile, has a parallax nearly twice as large as Algieba’s, which means it lies almost twice as close.
card.wonder: Through a small telescope the two golden giants appear side by side, one of the finest color pairs in the sky.
card.connect: Blue-white Regulus, at the foot of the Sickle, completes the color contrast.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos split the golden pair; binoculars show a single star and its chance neighbor, 40 Leonis.
card.deeper: Hipparcos gives 25.07 ± 0.52 mas for the combined pair (about 130 light-years). WDS lists STF 1424 AB at 4.8″ (magnitudes 2.37 and 3.64). The NASA Exoplanet Archive lists γ¹ Leo b (Han et al. 2010): period 429 days, minimum mass 8.8 Jupiters. 40 Leo (F6 IV-V) has a Gaia EDR3 parallax of 47.13 mas (about 69 light-years), so it is a foreground star.

card.question: Why is there fresh dust around Denebola?
card.answer: Something keeps making it, most likely asteroid- and comet-like bodies colliding and grinding each other down, a busier version of the debris belts in our own solar system.
card.glance: The white star at the tip of Leo’s tail, at the opposite end of the lion from Regulus.
card.whyHere: Denebola is a nearby white star at the lion’s tail, surrounded by dust that should not still be there.
card.see: Denebola marks the lion’s tail, east of the Sickle, a clean white point in binoculars. With Arcturus and Spica it forms the large Spring Triangle. Its dust shows only to infrared telescopes.
card.understand: Denebola is a hot white star about twice the Sun’s mass and 16 times as luminous, 36 light-years away. Infrared telescopes, which see warmth rather than light, detect more warmth around it than the star alone should give, the glow of dust. Dust like this cannot last, because starlight blows small grains out and drags others inward, so whatever we see now must be freshly made.
card.wonder: The light reaching you tonight left Denebola about 36 years ago, within many observers’ own lifetimes.
card.connect: The Spring Triangle’s other corners are orange Arcturus and blue-white Spica.
card.photoCaption: Visible-light photos show only the star; the dust appears in infrared measurements, not in any picture you could take.
card.deeper: Zorec & Royer (2012) give log Teff 3.931 (about 8,530 K), log L 1.21 and 1.93 solar masses. The Hipparcos parallax is 90.91 ± 0.52 mas (35.9 light-years). Near-infrared interferometry (Akeson et al. 2009) found an excess from hot dust close to the star, and Stock et al. (2010) modeled the disk’s structure; later work debates whether one, two or three dust belts are needed.

card.question: How do you know two close stars are truly partners?
card.answer: They must share a depth as well as a direction on the sky, and the pair of 19 Lyncis passes that test.
card.glance: A neat multiple star in the faint constellation Lynx, a bright point with a wider, fainter companion.
card.whyHere: 19 Lyncis is a young, hot multiple star and a fair test of what binoculars can and cannot split.
card.see: In faint Lynx, between the Big Dipper’s bowl and the Gemini twins, look for a fainter star about a tenth of a Moon-width from 19 Lyn; that wide companion is easy. The main pair is much tighter and stays merged in most binoculars.
card.understand: The two main stars are hot blue-white stars about three times the Sun’s mass. Gaia measures nearly the same parallax for both, putting them about 640 light-years away. Two stars this close on the sky and at the same depth are unlikely strangers.
card.wonder: The light you see set out in the late 1300s, while Chaucer was writing The Canterbury Tales.
card.connect: Wider, brighter doubles wait in the Big Dipper and Boötes.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos split all three stars; binoculars reliably show only the wide one.

card.question: How does a yellow giant compare with the Sun?
card.answer: Much bigger and only a little cooler, so it glows a slightly deeper yellow while pouring out far more light than the Sun.
card.glance: The star at the top of Leo’s Sickle, pale yellow in binoculars.
card.whyHere: Ras Elased Australis is a yellow giant much larger and brighter than the Sun, marking the top of the lion’s head.
card.see: Follow Leo’s Sickle, the backward question mark, up from Regulus to its top. In binoculars this star is a soft pale yellow; compare it with blue-white Regulus at the bottom of the same curve.
card.understand: It has left its long, steady adult life and swollen to about 21 times the Sun’s width, a size measured from its tiny disk with an interferometer. Its surface, near 5,300 K, is a little cooler than the Sun’s. That gives it a slightly deeper yellow tint.
card.wonder: Moved to its distance of about 250 light-years, the Sun would be too faint to see without binoculars.
card.connect: Regulus, at the foot of the Sickle, is the hot contrast.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a pale yellow point; the color difference from Regulus is easier to judge by eye.

card.question: Are there planetary systems like our own?
card.answer: 47 Ursae Majoris comes close, a Sun-like star whose giant planet keeps its distance as Jupiter does.
card.glance: A faint Sun-like star in southern Ursa Major, easy in binoculars and just visible to the eye from dark sites.
card.whyHere: 47 Ursae Majoris has a giant planet on a Jupiter-like orbit, one of the first signs that systems like ours exist.
card.see: It lies about 16 degrees south of Merak, the Big Dipper’s lower pointer star, in a sparse field. In binoculars it is a pale yellow point, worth comparing with white Merak if you start there.
card.understand: This is a star very like the Sun, about 46 light-years away. Three giant planets have been found from the wobble they cause in the star; the first, announced in 1996, takes about three years per orbit and weighs a few Jupiters. That was a more familiar arrangement than the scorching ‘hot Jupiters’ found around the same time.
card.wonder: Not one of its planets has ever been seen; only the star’s tiny back-and-forth motion gave them away.
card.connect: Lalande 21185, a red dwarf with planets of its own, lies about four and a half degrees south.
card.photoCaption: Photographs show only the star; its planets are known from Doppler measurements.

card.question: Which Big Dipper stars belong together?
card.answer: Merak, Phecda, Megrez, Alioth and Mizar still move as one family, while Dubhe and Alkaid are strangers passing through.
card.glance: The lower pointer star of the Big Dipper’s bowl, white in binoculars beside yellow-orange Dubhe.
card.whyHere: Merak is the lower pointer of the Big Dipper’s bowl, and one of the first stars caught moving in step with its neighbors.
card.see: Merak and Dubhe are the pointers to Polaris. In binoculars Merak is white and Dubhe yellow-orange, a sibling and a stranger side by side.
card.understand: In 1909 Ejnar Hertzsprung noticed that Merak and several other Dipper stars drift across the sky in the same direction at the same rate, like a flock. Modern measurements confirm a family moving through space together about 80 light-years away. The family’s age comes from interferometers that measured the shapes and sizes of its stars, including Merak’s two and a half Suns.
card.wonder: Stars of Merak’s mass are expected to end as white dwarfs inside glowing shells, much like the Owl Nebula two degrees away.
card.connect: Phecda, another sibling, is the next star around the bowl.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a white point; its family ties are known from motions measured over decades.

historyHook.text: In 1909 Ejnar Hertzsprung identified new members of a moving system made of the middle Big Dipper stars.

card.question: How much brighter does a star get for a little more mass?
card.answer: Far more than you might guess: Zosma has about twice the Sun’s mass but gives out about 29 times its light, and it will burn through its fuel correspondingly sooner.
card.glance: The white star on the lion’s back, in the triangle of stars that ends at Denebola.
card.whyHere: Zosma is a nearby white star, hotter and far brighter than the Sun, forming the lion’s hips.
card.see: Zosma and its neighbor Chertan form the lion’s back in Leo, with Denebola at the tail. In binoculars Zosma is white; compare it with golden Algieba in the mane.
card.understand: Zosma is about twice the Sun’s mass with a surface near 8,200 K. A heavier star squeezes its core harder, which heats it more, and fusion speeds up steeply with temperature. The result is that brightness climbs far faster than mass.
card.wonder: Its light left about 58 years ago, around the time astronauts first flew around the Moon.
card.connect: Denebola, the lion’s tail, is the next bright star east.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a plain white point.

card.question: How do astronomers date the Big Dipper’s family?
card.answer: By measuring the shapes and sizes of fast-spinning members like Phecda and fitting models to them, which together give the family an age of about 400 million years.
card.glance: The bowl star of the Big Dipper nearest the handle on the bottom side, white in binoculars.
card.whyHere: Phecda is another member of the Ursa Major family, sharing a birth and a path through space with Merak and Mizar.
card.see: Phecda is the lower bowl star on the handle side of the Big Dipper, white in binoculars. A faint galaxy, M109, lies just beside it, but that one needs a telescope.
card.understand: Linked telescopes have measured Phecda’s shape, and it spins fast enough to bulge at the equator. Once the bulge is measured, models can allow for the spin and read the star’s age from its size and temperature. Doing this for several family members dated the whole group.
card.wonder: Its light left about 83 years ago, around when the first nuclear reactor was switched on.
card.connect: Megrez, the faintest Dipper star, is the next sibling.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a white point; its flattened shape comes from interferometry, not images.

card.question: Are the stars of Corvus, the crow, neighbors in space?
card.answer: Minkar lies twice as far as its crow-mates, so the bird exists only from where we stand.
card.glance: The orange star at the western corner of Corvus, the crow.
card.whyHere: Minkar, the orange corner of the little crow of Corvus, raises a doubt about every constellation you have ever traced.
card.see: Corvus is the small four-star kite south-west of Spica, its main stars fitting in two or three binocular fields. Minkar is the most orange; compare it with blue-white Gienah about five degrees north.
card.understand: Minkar is an orange giant with a surface near 4,300 K. Its parallax puts it at about 320 light-years. That is at least twice as far as the other bright crow stars.
card.wonder: Its light left around the year 1700, not long after Newton showed that one law of gravity rules both apples and planets.
card.connect: Gienah, the crow’s brightest star, is a hot blue-white contrast.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an orange point.

superlatives.claim: the faintest of the seven Big Dipper stars

card.question: How bright is the faintest-looking Big Dipper star, really?
card.answer: Still about 28 times as bright as the Sun, so even the faintest-looking Dipper star would outshine our own many times over.
card.glance: The faintest Big Dipper star, where the handle joins the bowl.
card.whyHere: Megrez is a sibling in the Ursa Major family and the stepping stone to Messier 40, a famous false double.
card.see: Megrez is where the Big Dipper’s handle meets the bowl, white in binoculars. About one and a half degrees north-east lie the two faint stars of Winnecke 4 (M40); brace the binoculars to see them.
card.understand: Megrez is a white star about twice the Sun’s mass, born with Merak, Phecda, Alioth and Mizar about 400 million years ago. Linked telescopes show it spins fast enough to be flattened. It looks faintest of the seven because it is the least powerful, not because it is farther away.
card.wonder: Its light left around 1945, as the Second World War was ending.
card.connect: Beside it, M40 is two stars that only look like a pair.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a white point.

card.question: Why does Gienah look blue-white?
card.answer: Its surface is roughly twice as hot as the Sun’s, and a surface that hot glows blue-white.
card.glance: The brightest star of Corvus, a blue-white point at the crow’s north-western corner.
card.whyHere: Gienah is a hot blue-white star, a color contrast to the orange stars of the crow.
card.see: Find Corvus, the small kite of stars south-west of Spica. In binoculars Gienah is crisply blue-white; swing to orange Minkar or pale yellow Kraz to compare.
card.understand: A glowing object’s color tells its temperature, the way metal glows red, then yellow, then white as it heats. Gienah’s surface is about 12,400 K, which tips the balance of its light toward blue. It is a heavier star nearing the end of its long, steady adult life.
card.wonder: Its light left around 1870, while Mendeleev was arranging the elements into his periodic table.
card.connect: Algorab, across the crow, hides a faint companion.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white point.

card.question: Can binoculars catch a faint star in a bright star’s glare?
card.answer: Steady 10× binoculars can just reveal Algorab’s far fainter companion, while hand-held 7× usually lose it in the glare.
card.glance: A white star at the crow’s north-eastern corner, with a faint companion that steady 10× binoculars can just reveal.
card.whyHere: Algorab is a white star with a much fainter orange companion, a binocular test of separation and contrast.
card.see: Find Corvus, the small kite of stars south-west of Spica; Algorab is its north-eastern corner. With 10× binoculars on a tripod, look very close to it for a far fainter point. In hand-held 7× it usually hides in the glare.
card.understand: Algorab is a hot white star about two and a half times the Sun’s mass. The companion is a cool orange dwarf, and whether the two actually orbit each other is not settled. Seeing it is hard because a faint point beside a bright one drowns in the bright star’s scattered light.
card.wonder: Its light left around 1940, so it has been on its way for about a human lifetime.
card.connect: The Sombrero Galaxy lies about five and a half degrees north-north-east, a faint smudge under dark skies.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos split the pair easily; binoculars barely do.

card.question: Can a star the Sun’s color be very different from the Sun?
card.answer: Kraz glows nearly the Sun’s pale yellow, but as a giant it is far larger and pours out far more light.
card.glance: The pale yellow star at the crow’s south-eastern corner.
card.whyHere: Kraz is a bright giant, nearly the Sun’s color but far larger and more luminous.
card.see: Find Corvus, the small kite of stars south-west of Spica. In binoculars Kraz is pale yellow, about the Sun’s own color; compare it with blue-white Gienah across the crow.
card.understand: Its surface, near 5,100 K, is a little cooler than the Sun’s, so the colors are similar. But Kraz is a swollen giant, and from about 150 light-years it still shines as one of the crow’s brightest stars. The Sun at that distance would need binoculars to see.
card.wonder: Its light left around 1880, while Edison was perfecting the electric light bulb.
card.connect: Gienah, the hot star of the crow, makes the color contrast.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a pale yellow point.

card.question: Is the orange star at the tip of the Coma Cluster one of its members?
card.answer: γ Comae stands well in front of the cluster’s white stars and only lines up with them.
card.glance: An orange star at the northern tip of the sprawling Coma Star Cluster.
card.whyHere: γ Comae sits at the tip of the Coma Star Cluster like its leader, the obvious candidate for the family’s brightest member.
card.see: Find the Coma Star Cluster between Denebola and the Big Dipper’s handle, a loose spray of white stars filling the field. γ Com, at its northern tip, stands out as orange, the clue that it does not belong.
card.understand: Gaia’s parallaxes place the cluster’s members about 280 light-years away, but γ Com only about 170. It is a giant about 12 times the Sun’s width. It simply lies in front of the cluster along the same line of sight.
card.wonder: A Gaia census lists about 270 members of the cluster, and this star is not among them.
card.connect: The cluster’s white stars are the true siblings, all of one age.
card.photoCaption: Wide photos show γ Com as the only obviously orange star in the cluster’s field.

card.question: What lies beyond Vindemiatrix?
card.answer: Beyond it lie whole galaxies, the faint smudges of the Virgo cluster west of this nearby giant, whose light set out before there were humans.
card.glance: A yellowish star in Virgo’s northern arm, the gateway to the Virgo galaxy cluster.
card.whyHere: Vindemiatrix is a yellow giant in Virgo’s northern arm, and a signpost to something far more distant.
card.see: Vindemiatrix sits in Virgo’s northern arm, about 20 degrees west-south-west of Arcturus, pale yellow in binoculars. Under dark skies, sweep slowly west toward Denebola: the faint smudges along the way are galaxies far beyond our own.
card.understand: Vindemiatrix is a giant about 12 times the Sun’s width with a surface near 5,000 K. It lies roughly 110 light-years away. The galaxies behind it belong to the Virgo cluster, entire star systems so far away that this star is a next-door neighbor by comparison.
card.wonder: The star’s light is about a century old, and the galaxies’ light is tens of millions of years old.
card.connect: M49, among the brightest Virgo galaxies in binoculars, lies about eight degrees west-south-west.
card.photoCaption: Photos of this field show galaxies that binoculars reveal only as faint smudges.

card.question: What does a giant look like before it starts to pulse?
card.answer: Calm and steady, like γ Hydrae, a yellow giant that has not yet reached the restless stage its neighbor is in.
card.glance: A modest yellow star in Hydra’s long tail, the signpost for the variable R Hydrae.
card.whyHere: γ Hydrae is an ordinary yellow giant and the perfect comparison for its dramatic neighbor, R Hydrae.
card.see: Well below Spica, γ Hya is the brightest star in this stretch of Hydra. R Hya lies about two and a half degrees east, often in the same binocular field, so compare their colors: yellow against orange-red.
card.understand: γ Hya is a giant with a surface around 5,100 K, calm and steady, burning helium in its core. R Hydrae is further along the same road, cooler, larger and pulsing. The change comes once core helium runs out and the star must burn in thin, unstable shells.
card.wonder: Its light left around 1890, about when Van Gogh painted The Starry Night.
card.connect: R Hydrae, in the same field, shows that later stage.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a yellowish point.

card.question: What did one of the first planets around a Sun-like star look like?
card.answer: It looked nothing like Earth, for 70 Virginis’s planet is a heavyweight on a short, lopsided orbit.
card.glance: A faint yellowish star in northern Virgo, easy in binoculars, near τ Boötis.
card.whyHere: 70 Virginis hosts one of the first planets found around a Sun-like star, announced in 1996.
card.see: It lies about six degrees west-south-west of τ Boötis, itself west of Arcturus. In binoculars it is a pale yellow point among fainter stars.
card.understand: This Sun-like star is older than the Sun and has begun to swell, now nearly twice the Sun’s width. Its planet, at least seven times Jupiter’s mass, takes about 117 days per orbit. The orbit is stretched rather than round, another surprise for astronomers who had expected copies of our solar system.
card.wonder: Its light left in the late 1960s, a generation before anyone knew the planet was there.
card.connect: τ Boötis, nearby, hosts another planet announced the same year.
card.photoCaption: Photos show only the star; the planet is known from its pull on the star.

card.question: What does a star look like as it starts turning into a giant?
card.answer: Much like Muphrid, a little swollen and a little cooler, setting out on the road Arcturus has already traveled.
card.glance: A pale yellow-white star five degrees west of Arcturus.
card.whyHere: Muphrid is Arcturus’s neighbor in space, caught early in the change that Arcturus has already completed.
card.see: Sweep from Arcturus in Boötes about five degrees west to Muphrid. A wide field holds both: orange-gold beside pale yellow-white.
card.understand: Muphrid is just starting to swell as the hydrogen in its core runs low, and it is already about two and a half times the Sun’s width. Arcturus has gone much further down the same road, to a full giant about ten times wider than Muphrid. Side by side they are two frames of the same film.
card.wonder: The two are only about three light-years apart in space, closer to each other than the Sun is to any other star.
card.connect: Arcturus, beside it, shows where Muphrid is heading.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a pale yellow point.

card.question: Is Izar just a fainter Arcturus?
card.answer: Izar is no lesser copy, since it must pour out roughly three times as much light as Arcturus to look even this bright from so far away.
card.glance: An orange star in Boötes, single in binoculars, though telescopes reveal a lovely color pair.
card.whyHere: Izar looks like a fainter copy of nearby Arcturus, the same orange in a smaller dose.
card.see: In binoculars Izar is orange, like a dimmer copy of Arcturus ten degrees away in the kite of Boötes. Its blue-white companion is too close for binoculars.
card.understand: Izar lies about 200 light-years away, five or six times farther than Arcturus, though the parallax measurements disagree a little. Light spreads out as it travels, over an area that grows with the square of the distance, so from that far it would need around thirty times Arcturus’s output just to look as bright. It looks dimmer, but not by nearly that much.
card.wonder: Through a telescope its tiny companion looks blue against the orange primary, one reason it is nicknamed ‘the most beautiful’.
card.connect: δ and μ Boötis, nearby, are wide doubles your binoculars can split.

card.question: What would our Sun look like from δ Boötis’s distance?
card.answer: Almost exactly like δ Boötis’s faint companion, a modest point that binoculars split from the bright giant it travels with.
card.glance: A yellowish star in Boötes with a faint companion that binoculars split cleanly.
card.whyHere: δ Boötis is a wide, genuine double, a yellow giant and a faint Sun-like star traveling together.
card.see: δ Boo sits on the eastern side of the kite of Boötes, north-east of Arcturus. In 10× binoculars look just beside it for a much fainter point, about a sixteenth of a Moon-width away; it splits cleanly when you hold steady.
card.understand: The bright star is a giant about 11 times the Sun’s width, and its companion is a Sun-like dwarf. Gaia measures the same distance for both, about 120 light-years, so they belong together and orbit very slowly. The faint companion shows how dim a star like ours looks from here.
card.wonder: The light reaching you left δ Boötis around 1905, the year Einstein published special relativity.
card.connect: μ Boötis, a few degrees north-east, is another wide pair, and its faint star is double too.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the pair much as binoculars do.

card.question: How many stars hide in μ Boötis?
card.answer: There are three: binoculars split a bright white star from a faint companion, and a telescope splits that companion into two Sun-like stars.
card.glance: A white star in northern Boötes with a faint partner, itself a double.
card.whyHere: μ Boötis is a bright white star with a faint companion that binoculars can split.
card.see: μ Boo lies near the top of Boötes, a few degrees north-east of δ Boo. In 10× binoculars a much fainter star sits just south of it, about a sixteenth of a Moon-width away; hold steady to separate it from the glare.
card.understand: The bright star is white, about twice the Sun’s mass. The companion is a pair of Sun-like stars orbiting each other closely, too close for binoculars. All three share the same distance and motion through space, the two tests of a real family.
card.wonder: The light you see left these stars a little over a century ago, around the time Einstein was rethinking what light is.
card.connect: ν Boötis, a few degrees north, looks like another pair but is not.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the wide pair as binoculars do; the close pair needs high magnification.

card.question: Is the matched pair of ν Boötis a real couple?
card.answer: It is a match made only by perspective: a distant giant and a nearer white star that happen to line up.
card.glance: Two stars about a third of a Moon-width apart in northern Boötes, one orange and one white.
card.whyHere: ν Boötis looks like the best-matched pair in Boötes, two stars of equal brightness side by side.
card.see: Start at Nekkar, the star at the top of the kite of Boötes, and sweep east. Binoculars show orange ν¹ and white ν² side by side, nearly equal in brightness.
card.understand: Whether the two belong together is something Gaia can settle by parallax, the tiny shift of each star as Earth circles the Sun. Those shifts put ν¹, an orange giant, nearly 1,000 light-years away, and ν², a white star, about 440. Light fades with the square of distance, so to look equally bright from more than twice as far, the orange star must give out roughly five times as much light.
card.wonder: The orange star’s light set out around the year 1050, about when Chinese astronomers recorded the supernova that left us the Crab Nebula.
card.connect: μ Boötis, nearby, is a pair that really does belong together.

contexts.text: A loose family of stars born together about 400 million years ago. Its core forms five of the Big Dipper’s seven stars; Dubhe and Alkaid are not members.

edge.HR4301>HR5191: From one end of the Dipper to the other you go from {prev}, a cool yellow-orange giant, to {next}, a hot blue-white youngster, and both are outsiders to the family between them.
edge.DS-MizarAlcor>Mel111: The Ursa Major family has scattered across the sky, while the Coma Star Cluster still holds together and shows what such a family looks like before it disperses.
edge.HR2784>DS-MizarAlcor: Like {prev}, Mizar and Alcor nest pairs within pairs, and here your eyes alone can split the widest gap, though whether Mizar and Alcor themselves are bound is still argued.
edge.HR4660>DS-Winnecke4: Just off {prev}, a family star close to us, sit two faint stars that look like a pair, yet they lie far beyond it and far from each other.

edge.HR5733>HR5763: {prev} is a real triple whose stars travel together, while a few degrees north the two stars of ν Boötis look like a matched pair, though one lies more than twice as far away as the other.

edge.HR5506>STAR-Arcturus: {prev} looks like a fainter copy of {next}, with the same orange color, but it is five times farther away, so it must be the more powerful star.
edge.STAR-Arcturus>HR5056: {prev} weighs about as much as the Sun and will end quietly, but carry the arc on to {next} and you find a star more than ten times heavier, burning so fast that it will end as a supernova.
edge.HR5056>STAR-Arcturus: Blue-white {prev} and orange {next} hang at opposite ends of the same arc, the hot and cool ends of the stellar thermometer in one sweep of the sky.
edge.HR5235>STAR-Arcturus: {prev} has only just begun to swell as its core runs low on hydrogen, while {next} has finished that change and become a full giant about ten times wider.
edge.HR5235>STAR-Arcturus.neighbor: {prev} and {next} are real neighbors, only about three light-years apart in space.
edge.STAR-Arcturus>STAR-LaSuperba: {prev} is an aging giant, and {next} shows a later chapter for stars a little heavier, in which carbon made deep inside has reached the surface and turned the star deep red.
edge.STAR-Arcturus>M3.population: {prev} is an old star passing through from the galaxy’s thick disk, and {next} is older still, hundreds of thousands of stars that formed in the galaxy’s youth and orbit far out in its halo.
edge.HR4534>STAR-Vega: Like {prev}, {next} is a hot white star wrapped in dust from colliding rocks, two nearby examples of planetary leftovers.
edge.STAR-LaSuperba>DS-AlpCVn: Swing from deep-red {prev} to white {next}, a few degrees away, and you pass from one of the coolest stars you can see to one of the hotter ones, reading the stellar thermometer by color.
edge.HR4785>STAR-LaSuperba: {prev} is a Sun-like star in its long, steady prime, while {next}, a few degrees away, is a giant near the end of a much later stage, cooled to a deep red.
edge.HR4785>DS-AlpCVn: Pale yellow {prev}, much like the Sun, sits beside white {next}, which is about twice as hot at the surface.
edge.DS-AlpCVn>HR4905: {prev} gave its name to a class of spotted, magnetic stars, and {next}, the brightest Dipper star, belongs to it, its light flickering slightly as patches of unusual elements rotate into view.
edge.HR3541>STAR-LaSuperba: {prev} and {next} are both carbon stars, late-stage giants reddened by carbon dredged up from inside.
edge.M44>HR3541: The Beehive’s brightest stars are still in their steady adult lives, but a few degrees away {next} shows a late stage that stars of similar mass can reach, a carbon-rich giant shedding its outer layers.
edge.HR3882>HR3982: Hot, young, fast-spinning {next} and cool, dying, pulsing {prev} sit only five degrees apart in Leo.
edge.HR3882>HR5080: {prev} and {next} are both Mira stars, giants in their last stage, swelling and shrinking over most of a year.
edge.HR5020>HR5080: Calm, yellow {prev} is a giant in its middle years, while next door {next} has moved on to the final, unstable stage, cooler, larger and pulsing.
edge.HR424>DS-DeltaCep: {prev} and {next} are both Cepheids, stars whose pulse rate reveals their true power and so unlocks the distances to other galaxies.
edge.HR3982>HR4057: From blue-white {prev} to golden {next}, a few steps up the Sickle, you stay in one constellation but cross a wide range of surface temperatures.
edge.STAR-Alphard>HR3982: Orange {prev} stands alone in Hydra while blue-white {next} anchors Leo, so swing between them to read the stellar thermometer.
edge.HR3873>HR3982: The top and bottom of Leo’s Sickle make a color pair, pale yellow {prev} above and blue-white {next} below.
edge.HR4357>HR4534: {prev} and {next}, the lion’s hip and tail, are both nearby white stars somewhat heavier than the Sun.
edge.HR3982>STAR-Sirius: The hidden partner of {prev} is turning into a white dwarf, while {next} already has one, the Sun’s fate seen by proxy.
edge.HR4630>HR4757.los: {prev} and {next} both outline the crow, but {prev} is about three and a half times farther away, so the bird is a trick of perspective.
edge.HR4662>HR4630: Blue-white {prev} and orange {next} share the crow, a hot star and a cool giant five degrees apart.
edge.HR4662>HR4786: Across the crow from blue-white {prev}, {next} glows pale yellow, about the color of the Sun.
edge.HR4757>M104: From {prev}, a star whose light left within living memory, you step to {next}, a whole galaxy whose light left before humans existed.
edge.HR4932>M49: {prev} is a nearby giant, and a sweep west brings you to {next}, an entire galaxy in the Virgo Cluster, far beyond the Milky Way.
edge.HR4737>Mel111: {prev} looks like the brightest member of the Coma Cluster, but its orange color gives it away, because it lies well in front of the white sibling stars.

edge.HR5191>M51: From {prev}, about a hundred light-years away, slide a few degrees to {next}, a whole spiral galaxy so far away that its light left long before humans existed.
edge.HD95735>HR4550: {prev} is a quiet red dwarf of our own disk and one of the Sun’s nearest neighbors, while {next}, nearby on the sky, is a visitor from the galaxy’s ancient halo racing through on a steep orbit.
edge.HR4550>STAR-Arcturus: Both {prev} and {next} are outsiders passing through the Sun’s neighborhood at high speed, members of older populations of the galaxy.
edge.HR4550>HD140283: {prev} and {next} are both halo stars, poor in heavy elements because they formed before the galaxy had been enriched.
edge.HR4550>M3: {prev} is a lone halo star passing by, and {next} is a whole swarm of halo stars that has held together for most of the galaxy’s history.
edge.HR4550>NAME-BarnardsStar: {prev} and {next} are both nearby stars that visibly shift against the background within a human lifetime of careful measurement.
edge.HD95735>DS-61Cyg: Like {prev}, {next} is one of the Sun’s near neighbors, a small, cool dwarf of the kind that is most common in the galaxy.
edge.HR4277>HD95735: {prev} is a Sun-like star with giant planets, while four and a half degrees south {next} is a red dwarf whose known planets are small, so planets form around very different stars.
edge.HR4277>HR4785: {prev} and {next} are both stars much like the Sun, yellow, steady and in the prime of their lives.
edge.HR3522>HR4277: {prev} and {next} each host several planets, all found from the wobble they cause in their star.
edge.HR5185>HR5072: {prev} and {next} sit only a few degrees apart, and both of their planets were announced in the same year, among the first found around Sun-like stars.
edge.HR3522>HR8729: The first planet of {prev} was announced only a year after the planet of {next}, the first ever found around a Sun-like star.
edge.HR424>HR5563: {prev} and {next} have both served as the pole star, because Earth’s slow wobble moves the sky’s pivot from one to the other over thousands of years.
edge.HR5563>HR4057: {prev} and {next} are both giant stars with giant planets, so planets can survive, at least for a while, around stars that have already swollen.
edge.HR5185>HR3522: {prev} and {next} both have planets that race around them in days, far closer than Mercury is to the Sun.
edge.HR5185>HR8729: The planet of {prev} is a ‘hot Jupiter’ like the one found around {next}, a giant world baking close to its star, a type nobody expected before 1995.

edge.STAR-Alphard>HR3882: {prev} is a steady orange giant, and {next}, in Leo, shows the next and last giant stage, pulsing, cooling and losing its outer layers.
edge.HR4534>HR5056: Two corners of the Spring Triangle face two fates: {prev}, about twice the Sun’s mass, will end as a white dwarf, while the larger star of {next}, more than ten times the Sun’s mass, will explode.
edge.HR5080>STAR-Mira: {prev} and {next} are both Mira stars, dying giants that swell and fade over most of a year.
edge.HR424>HR5056: {prev} and {next} were both weighed the same way, by timing a companion’s orbit, the only direct way to measure a star’s mass.
